title: Did the Greeks have no word for blue? COLOR WORDS

entries.note: Only became a specific colour word in English in the 1300s, from a French word that could also mean pale, light or blonde; often the last colour languages name.
Homer's description of the sea, cited as a sign the Greeks had no word for [[see:blue]], evoking brightness rather than blueness.
Found in Homer, when it simply meant dark; in modern Greek it means blue, and it gave English [[gave:cyan]].
English colour word that comes from Greek [[from:kyanos]].
Expressing several concepts with the same word, as many languages do with one colour term covering both blue and green.
Word for blue in many Celtic languages that can also describe the colour of grass; the hosts don't know whether it's related to glass.
Italian treats azure as distinct from blue, so an Italian would say the sky is azzurro rather than blue.
Named after a flower called pink, which is unusual because other languages call it something like rose; Rob argues pink is really just light red.
Jess would always call this colour teal where her husband would say green or blue; Rob only recently began seeing it as teal.
From a very old root meaning burnt, either charred or blazing, so it shares a root with [[same-root:blank]], [[same-root:bleak]] and [[same-root:bleach]].
From the French word for white, [[from:blanc]], and shares an old root with [[same-root:black]].
Means very dark and comes from the same root as [[same-root:black]].
Means to lighten something, yet comes from the same root as [[same-root:black]].
Old English word for black, related to German [[same-root:schwarz]]; it meant darkness or absence of light, gave [[gave:swarthy]], and was pushed out by [[see:black]] in Middle English.
German for black, given as related to [[same-root:swart]].
From [[from:swart]]; it carries an edge of colourism, and Jess avoids it as outdated and found mostly in literature.
From a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to shine whose k became h; like [[see:hwæt]], Old English hw- became w; shares its root with [[same-root:wheat]].
First word of [[see:Beowulf]], an example of Old English hw- words that came to start with w, like [[see:white]].
Named for the bright white colour of the grain once it's milled; shares its root with [[same-root:white]].

Its Old English predecessor covered light things, including green, grey, white, light blue and daytime skies; from Germanic [[from:*gelwaz]], like German [[same-root:gelb]]; American slang for cowardly.
German for yellow, from the same Germanic root as [[same-root:yellow]].
American term for cowardly; the hosts can't explain where it comes from and ask viewers to say in the comments.
From the French for yellow; the condition was often blamed on an imbalance of humours such as [[see:melancholy]], [[see:sanguine]] and [[see:phlegm]].
One of the humours; Jess believes the word means dark bile.
The humour of blood, which became a word for red; it could describe having too much blood or being in love.
Another of the humours; Jess can't recall which imbalance it was said to cause.
An earlier American way of calling someone cowardly; nobody has worked out what the streak refers to.
Comes not from the fossilised tree resin but from [[from:ambergris]], although the two share an Arabic root.
French for grey amber, a waxy substance the hosts think comes from sperm whales' bile; it gave [[gave:amber]].
Means pertaining to amber, from Greek [[from:elektron]], because early static electricity experiments rubbed wool on [[see:amber]].
Named after [[from:Tyrian purple]], a costly dye from murex sea snail shells, so rare that purple became the colour of royalty.
Audacious, royally elaborate prose, named after the royal associations of [[see:purple]].
Means pink like flesh, related to [[same-root:carnation]] and [[same-root:carnivore]]; [[see:Lady Macbeth]] uses it to mean blood red in 'multitudinous seas incarnadine'.
The flower's name is related to [[same-root:incarnadine]].
Related to [[same-root:incarnadine]], which means pink like flesh.
Named after the wine from the [[from:Burgundy]] region.
Colour named after the stone.
Named after the fruit and discussed on the podcast before; Old English called it [[see:yellow-red]], Middle English [[see:citrine]] or [[see:saffron]].
The Old English way of naming [[see:orange]].
A Middle English name for [[see:orange]], named after a fruit or plant.
A Middle English name for [[see:orange]], named after a plant.
Originally a tangerine orange, meaning an orange from [[from:Tangier]], and now used on its own for the colour.
Named after a dye from [[from:India]].
Named after [[from:Magenta]], a northern Italian town where the dye could be obtained.
Named after the botanist [[from:Leonhart Fuchs]].
Named after an insect, [[from:Kermes ilicis]], which was crushed to make the dye; the hosts identify it with [[see:cochineal]].
Insect the hosts identify with the one crushed for [[see:crimson]] dye; French uses the same word, [[same-root:coccinelle]], for the ladybird.
French for a ladybird, the same word as [[same-root:cochineal]], though ladybirds were never crushed to make [[see:crimson]] dye.
A brownish purple that literally means flea colour, perhaps after the stain of a flea bite rather than the flea itself.
Describes very fine spotty patterns on horses and dogs, and once discolourations on human skin; linked to the flea-bite sense of [[see:puce]].
From the French word for a mole.
Spelled gray more in America and grey in the UK because Old English wrote it with [[see:ash]] and a final g that became y, like [[see:day]] and [[see:way]].
Old English letter written as a and e back to back, used in the old spelling of [[see:grey]].
Like [[see:grey]], it once ended in a g that turned into a y.
Like [[see:grey]], it once ended in a g that turned into a y.
A folk etymology: from Old English [[from:grighund]], with hund meaning dog, later misread as named after the colour [[see:grey]].
Discussed in the hosts' earlier episode about [[see:portmanteau]]s.
The topic of an earlier episode of the podcast.
Meant grey-coloured or old long before [[see:grizzly]] became associated with bears.
Means partially grey; grizzly bears may be named for their silver-tipped fur, or the name may be a misspelling of [[from?:grisly]], meaning gory and brutal.
Shares an ancient root with [[same-root:graze]], [[same-root:grass]] and [[same-root:grow]], as in 'the cow grazed on freshly grown green grass'.
Shares an ancient root with [[same-root:green]].
Shares an ancient root with [[same-root:green]].
Shares an ancient root with [[same-root:green]].
Literally means green, used as a pun on the words that share a root with [[see:green]].
Homer's word for the sea, usually translated gleaming or silvery, also used for blue, grey or green eyes; it gave [[gave:glaucoma]].
Comes from Greek [[from:glaukos]].
Not really a colour name: a yellow-flowered European plant fermented into indigo-blue dye, a staple by the 1400s; the blue-skinned Celts idea rests on [[see:vitrum]].
A Roman glass with a blue or green tint; [[see:Julius Caesar]] wrote that Britons dyed their skin with it, and it was sometimes translated as [[see:woad]].
One theory links it to the permanent colour of the sky, another to the permanence of blue dye.
A yellow dye used alongside [[see:woad]] in the medieval era.
A red dye used alongside [[see:woad]] in the medieval era.
Originally a word for rich cloth of any colour, and now a specific colour.

Very similar across Indo-European languages and the first colour named after light and dark; once also covered orange, purple and pink; shares a root with [[same-root:ruddy]], [[same-root:rusty]] and [[same-root:ruby]].
Shares an ancient root with [[same-root:red]].
Shares an ancient root with [[same-root:red]].
Shares an ancient root with [[same-root:red]].
One theory says orange-haired people are called redheads because English had [[see:red]] but no word yet for [[see:orange]].
A blue and a steel-grey metal, from German [[from:Kobold]], household goblin; silver miners' term for rock laced with arsenic and sulphur that could make you sick.
German for a goblin, which Jess associates with Dungeons and Dragons; it gave [[gave:cobalt]].
Its name has a story very similar to that of [[see:cobalt]].
Discussed on the podcast before; the hosts joke about doing a whole episode on Nicks.
Comes from the bark used for tanning leather.
From a root meaning to shine, like [[same-root:burnish]]; its meaning flipped from shiny to dusky and then to the colour of mud.
To polish something until it shines; it originally meant the same thing as [[same-root:brown]].
Probably related to Latin [[from?:lavare]], to wash, since the plant scented washing, though it may be closer to words like [[same-root?:livid]].
From [[from:marron]], French for a chestnut; unrelated to [[unrelated:marooning]] or the Bugs Bunny-era insult.
French for a chestnut that also simply means brown; it gave [[gave:maroon]].
A Bugs Bunny-era insult, saved for a future episode and unrelated to the colour.
Leaving someone stranded on an island; unrelated to the colour [[unrelated:maroon]].
For eyes, originally red-brown, now more green-brown, after hazelnuts; [[see:Mercutio]] says [[see:Benvolio]] would quarrel with someone cracking nuts because he has hazel eyes.
From a Greek word meaning thoroughly white or white mixed with colours; first a costly patterned silk, then fine napkins shaped like a baby's diaper.
